To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) intrauterine exposure to maternal diabetes confers a higher risk for type 2 (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus and obesity in the progeny than does exposure to paternal diabetes; 2) the risk of type 2 diabetes is increased by 3.7-fold in offspring of diabetic pregnancies compared with offspring of nondiabetics (P < 0.01); and 3) the mean body mass index of the offspring is higher by 2.6

the risk for developing type 2 diabetes in adulthood and for developing obesity in childhood is higher in siblings born to a diabetic mother than in siblings born to the same woman before her diabetes diagnosis.
Intrauterine environment per se is a risk factor for type 2 DM and obesity in offspring.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of intrauterine environment on the development of diabetes in the offspring and the possible mechanisms involved.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie the association of maternal diabetes with increased risk of obesity and diabetes in the offspring.
the role of the fetal environment in determining susceptibility to diabetes in later life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
intrauterine exposure to maternal diabetes per se conveys a high risk for development of diabetes and for obesity in offspring in addition to risk attributable to genetic factor alone.
intrauterine exposure to maternal diabetes per se confers a higher risk for type 2 and obesity in the progeny.

intrauterine exposure to maternal diabetes is associated with increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease in offspring, and that these effects are independent of genetic factors and the effects of maternal obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intrauterine environment can influence the risk for type 2 and obesity in the adult offspring.
intrauterine exposure to maternal diabetes is associated with excess risk for the development both of type 2 diabetes mellitus and of obesity.
the intrauterine environment is important for the development of type 2 diabetes in the offspring.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intrauterine exposure to a diabetic environment is a major determinant of the risk of diabetes and obesity later in life.
the intrauterine environment has an important impact on the risk of diabetes and obesity.
intrauterine exposure to maternal diabetes is associated with excess risk for diabetes and obesity in children.
